name: Student Work and Privacy
title: Student Work and Privacy
answer: The idea of student work and privacy means that essays, projects, and test answers are education records, so pasting them into a general chat tool shares those records with a company the district has no agreement with. The safe path is to use only tools covered by a signed data privacy agreement and to check the district's approved list before uploading any student work. This matters because helpful feedback can come with a real privacy cost, and removing names does not always protect a student's identity.

sections.body: This idea is about protecting student work when teachers use digital tools for feedback and grading. The problem is that student essays, projects, and test answers are part of education records under FERPA, and a teacher who pastes them into a general chat tool may share those records with a company the district has no agreement with. The feedback might be useful, but the privacy cost is real. The safe path is to use tools covered by a signed data privacy agreement, such as approved district tools like Gemini for Education or a school license for MagicSchool. Teachers should check the district's approved list before uploading any student work, and if a tool is not on the list, student work should not go into it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a teacher checks the district's approved list before putting any student work into a tool. If the tool is covered by a signed data privacy agreement, it can be used for feedback and grading, and if it is not on the list, the work should not be uploaded. The text does not give separate steps by grade band, so the same rule applies across grades: use approved tools and keep unapproved tools out of student work. Teachers should also consider what the work reveals before sharing it, because an essay about family, neighborhood, or personal experience may identify a student even without a name. When in doubt, the teacher should use an approved tool or give the feedback personally.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label, study, figure, or finding for this idea. It does not cite research on privacy outcomes or on the use of approved tools. The guidance rests on practice and on the FERPA description from Chapter 3, not on a research study. So this idea should be read as practical advice about handling student work rather than as an evidence-backed claim.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear: removing names is not always enough, because personal writing can identify a student without a name. Teachers should think about what the work reveals before sharing it with any tool, and when in doubt they should use an approved tool or give the feedback themselves. The decision to upload student work stays with the teacher, who must check the district's approved list and avoid tools not on it. Students should also know how their work is handled, and a short note at the start of the year can explain which tools the teacher uses for feedback and how the district protects student information. Families appreciate knowing, and that transparency builds the trust that makes these tools acceptable.
